name: Peabody Energy

summary.text: Peabody Energy, based in St. Louis, was the world's largest publicly traded coal company. In November 2015 it settled a two-year New York Attorney General investigation under the Martin Act by agreeing to revise its securities disclosures about climate-regulation risk, with no penalty and no admission of wrongdoing. Its 2016 Chapter 11 filings listed as creditors a number of organisations and individuals active in disputing climate science or opposing renewable-energy policy, including Willie Soon, ALEC, CFACT and the Edison Electric Institute.

facts.claim: On November 8-9, 2015 Peabody agreed with the New York Attorney General to revise its financial disclosures to reflect the potential impact of climate-change regulation on its business, after a two-year investigation into its SEC filings.
facts.quote: The settlement followed a two-year investigation by the NYAG into Peabody's failure to disclose climate-related financial risks in SEC filings.

sources.publisher: Columbia Law School, Sabin Center Climate Law Blog
sources.title: Peabody Energy Agrees to Update SEC Filings to Acknowledge Financial Risks of Climate Change Policies
Peabody Settlement Shows Muscle of Law Now Aimed at Exxon

facts.claim: The Attorney General found that Peabody had repeatedly said in public filings that it could not predict how climate regulation would affect its business while its internal studies showed revenue could fall sharply if coal were targeted.
facts.quote: the company repeatedly denied in public filings it could predict how potential climate change regulations would affect its business, even though its internal studies showed revenue could tumble

sources.title: Peabody Settlement Shows Muscle of Law Now Aimed at Exxon

facts.claim: The settlement involved no admission or denial of wrongdoing and no financial penalty, and was brought under the Martin Act (General Business Law Article 23-A, Section 352) and Executive Law Section 63(12).
facts.quote: There was no admission or denial of wrongdoing and no financial penalty.

Peabody agrees to fuller disclosures of climate change impacts

facts.claim: The agreed amendments focused on Peabody's references to the International Energy Agency's World Energy Outlook scenarios and its ability to estimate the impact of prospective laws.
facts.quote: Peabody agreed to enhance its disclosure around all the published scenarios when referencing the IEA's World Energy Outlook.

sources.title: Peabody agrees to fuller disclosures of climate change impacts

facts.claim: Peabody's 2016 bankruptcy filings listed creditors including Willie Soon, Heartland Institute staffer James Taylor, ALEC, the 60 Plus Association, the Edison Electric Institute, the George C. Marshall Institute, CFACT, the Center for the Study of Carbon Dioxide and Global Change, Roy Spencer and Friends of Science.
facts.quote: EcoWatch listed ALEC among a raft of anti-renewable legislation groups that were creditors, alongside the 60 Plus Association, Edison Electric Institute, and George C. Marshall Institute.

openQuestions: Site claim (settled; corrected statements, no fine): supported.
The date of Peabody's Chapter 11 filing (April 2016) was not confirmed from the sources used; the creditor-list reporting is from June 2016.
Creditor-list entries show amounts owed at filing, not past grant totals; CMD/EcoWatch/DeSmog are advocacy publishers.
